16/S0/F0.text: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an extended reality (XR) system.

16/S0/F1.text: Keeping track of motion in the physical world is a crucial part of any extended reality (XR) system, more importantly in virtual reality (VR) systems.

16/S0/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion in the virtual world.

16/S0/F3.text: In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view.

16/S0/F4.text: Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.

16/S1/F0.text: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

16/S1/F1.text: Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

16/S1/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

16/S1/F3.text: In virtual reality (VR), eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.

16/S1/F4.text: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.

16/S1/F5.text: For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience.

16/S1/F6.text: A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

16/S1/F7.text: Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in augmented reality (AR), but also important in virtual reality (VR).

16/S1/F8.text: In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

16/S1/F9.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked.

16/S1/F10.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience.

16/S1/F11.text: In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

16/S2/F0.text: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

16/S2/F1.text: Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking.

16/S2/F2.text: In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.

16/S2/F3.text: Most virtual reality (VR) headsets today that use external sensors fall under outside-in tracking.

16/S2/F4.text: Outside-in tracking is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed and works only when the user is in that environment within the sensor range, whereas inside-out tracking has no such restriction because the user wears the sensors or the sensors are attached to the user.

16/S2/F5.text: Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors required for tracking are located within the device used for the experience, such as the head-mounted display (HMD) in virtual reality (VR), which is more common, so no other external devices are needed.

16/S2/F6.text: Examples of inside-out tracking are Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, and Qualcomm VR820.

16/S3/F0.text: There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.

16/S3/F1.text: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

16/S3/F2.text: In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

16/S3/F3.text: In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

16/S3/F4.text: In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

16/S3/F5.text: In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.
